questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I decided to go to China because of a personal connection to the country, as well as the unique academic opportunity to study at one of China’s top universities.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The first days, spent navigating and organizing all the practical practicalities, were the most challenging. During this time, I relied heavily on my Mandarin-speaking friends.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
During dorm registration, there were initially no English-speaking staff available, although I later realized this was likely a matter of bad timing, as I did meet English-speaking staff members on other occasions. However, very little information was provided regarding when, where, and how to complete the registration process. Much of this information I received through other exchange students, who shared their own experiences and guidance.

My contact person at Fudan University also repeatedly provided incorrect information. For example, we were given the wrong dates for dormitory sign-up, directed to the wrong building on orientation day, and were not informed in advance about the requirement to purchase insurance. Despite these challenges, everything worked out in the end. Since all of the exchange law students shared the same contact person, we were equally confused, which fortunately allowed us to support one another and find comfort in the shared experience.

However, I do not blame Fudan University as an institution. Some of my friends, who were also exchange students in other programs, had excellent orientation experiences. Their contact persons were highly supportive, organizing trips, social activities, and providing clear guidance throughout the process. This showed me that the overall experience largely depended on the specific faculty and coordinator rather than the university itself.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: Applying for campus accommodation was stressful, mainly because my contact person provided incorrect information throughout the process. In addition, the housing options were limited. However, I was fortunate to secure a single room with my own bathroom in the main building. Other students were placed in supplementary buildings with roommates, but they also seemed satisfied with their living arrangements. Friends of mine who chose not to live on campus were still able to find accommodation without too much difficulty, although it was generally more expensive.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: Fudan University has the best on-campus facilities I have ever experienced. The university offers very affordable food, numerous large canteens, fitness centers, spacious outdoor areas, and convenient warehouse services for collecting and returning packages—an important feature in China, where online shopping is extremely common. The campus is also easy to navigate, making daily life both practical and comfortable for students

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I would highly recommend applying for on-campus accommodation. Some of my closest friendships during my exchange were formed through living in the dorms. Socially, it made a significant difference—living on campus made spontaneous meetups and casual hangouts much easier, whether it was visiting each other’s rooms, going to the canteen together, or working out at the gym. It created a strong sense of community and made student life much more enjoyable.

It is also relatively affordable. For international students, the main accommodation options are:
- Single room – Includes a private bathroom and is located in the main building, which has 23 floors and elevators.
- Double room – Two students share one room and one bathroom, also located in the main building.
- Shared apartment – Four students each have their own private room with a lockable door, while sharing two bathrooms. These are located in the supplementary building, which is older and less modern than the main building, has no elevator, and consists of 7 floors.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: At first, my contact person responded quite quickly, but the main issue was that she went on vacation right before the most important period—during registration, dorm applications, and the general arrival process. Many of my friends, who were also exchange law students, experienced similar problems with her communication. She provided incorrect information to several of us, which created unnecessary confusion and stress during an already challenging transition period.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Although my contact person was not particularly helpful, I was introduced during the first or second week to local students who showed us around and helped us settle in. One of them in particular was an enormous help, and I found myself reaching out to him far more often than to my official contact person. In general, the Chinese local students were incredibly kind, welcoming, and always willing to help, which made the transition much easier and contributed greatly to a positive exchange experience

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer:
You are generally guaranteed a place in all the classes you sign up for, which is a major advantage and makes course selection much less stressful. However, it is important to be aware that the curriculum provided during the registration process can change significantly once the semester begins. In my experience, professors have far more discretion over the course structure and assessment methods than what I am used to in Denmark.

For instance, one course was initially described as having an essay-based exam, but it ultimately became a written sit-in exam instead. In other courses, additional tests and assignments were introduced that had not been mentioned in the original curriculum. When I asked my contact person about these changes, she explained that professors are free to decide such matters themselves, and that the curriculum sent out beforehand should only be considered tentative.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try not to stress too much—everything usually works out in the end. One piece of advice I would definitely give is to make friends with people who speak Mandarin, especially if you do not speak the language yourself. It has been incredibly helpful for me on many occasions, both in practical situations and in making everyday life much easier.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
I spent less time preparing for classes than I normally would at home. Most of my courses were coursework-based, meaning that the final assessment primarily consisted of an essay. Presentations or midterm exams were often included as well, usually accounting for around 10–30% of the final grade, while attendance and class participation made up a smaller percentage. However, the essay remained the main component in most courses.

The essays were challenging because very little guidance was provided regarding expectations, structure, or grading criteria. It often felt like writing several mini bachelor’s assignments, and it was difficult to assess what academic level was required in order to achieve a good grade.

However, after receiving my grades, I found that the assessments were more generous than I had expected. Despite the common perception that academic grading in China is particularly strict, my experience was that the professors were fair and, in many cases, quite lenient.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
The teaching style varied greatly depending on the course. In some classes, professors would frequently cold-call students, while in others we had fixed seating arrangements so attendance could be monitored more closely. This was important because in certain courses, missing more than a specific number of classes would automatically result in a failing grade. There was little to none groupwork.

At the same time, it was also my impression that many professors genuinely cared about their students. If you attended classes regularly and participated actively, they were often very kind, supportive, and understanding. For instance, I became quite sick during the exam period. Most of my professors were extremely understanding and provided me with extensions.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Chinese Environment and Resources Law = The professor cold calls, but really sweet if you participate.
Chinese Legal Culture = The professor seemed to enjoy lecturing at length without much focus on student engagement or practical discussion. I would not particularly recommend this course, as it did not feel especially relevant as a law course and lacked the academic depth I had expected.
Chinese Pratice on International Law = The professor was at times difficult to understand, but the overall atmosphere of the class was very relaxed. The professor was extremely easygoing and seemed to prioritize making students feel comfortable rather than creating unnecessary pressure. As a result, it felt like almost everyone received an A in the course. 
Chinese Civil Law = I absolutely loved this professor - highly intelligent, engaging, and clearly passionate about the subject. The class was very interesting. I strongly recommend this course.
Chinese Commercial Arbitration = Very interesting if you like arbitration. 
Introduction to Chinese Law = I had two professors for this course—one was very stoic and reserved, while the other was much more engaging and dynamic in class. I was told that the latter also often participates in a Chinese television show, as a debater (I think(?)), which added an interesting dimension to his teaching style. I would recommend this course, as it was spread over two days, had a very relaxed structure.
Chinese language I = I did not receive credits for this course, as it is not a law course. The course was taught by my absolute favorite professor during the exchange. She was incredibly engaging, kind, and genuinely enjoyable to learn from. Her teaching style made the class both fun and memorable. I strongly recommend this course!

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all the courses above, with the exception of Chinese Legal Culture

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Honestly, there were no major unexpected fees. However, it is important to remember that the university requires students to purchase mandatory insurance. If I remember correctly, the cost was around 800 RMB, so it is worth keeping that in mind when budgeting for the semester.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: One of the biggest financial advantages was how inexpensive everyday life was, especially on campus. The canteen food was incredibly cheap, even compared to the generally low food prices in China. Online shopping was also very inexpensive, and costs for travelling, hotels, and high-speed trains were surprisingly low as well. This made it much easier to enjoy both daily student life and weekend trips without constantly worrying about expenses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There were many activities, clubs, and student societies available on campus—almost every type of club imaginable seemed to exist at the university. This made it easy for students to get involved beyond academics and meet people with shared interests.

One memorable event was a cooking competition where chefs from university canteens across the country came to showcase their skills. 

The university also organized various trips, tours, and social activities for exchange students, although the extent of this depended greatly on the specific faculty and program. Some faculties were much more active in creating these opportunities than others.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join a club!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
One of the most important parts of studying abroad in China is to travel as much as possible. One of my professors said during the first or second week that, in order to truly understand China and Chinese law, you need to experience the culture firsthand rather than only read about it in books. I found this to be absolutely true.

For nature and landscapes, I would highly recommend Zhangjiajie, Yangshuo and Jiuzhaigou. These places offer some of the most breathtaking scenery.

For city experiences, I would especially recommend Chongqing, Shenzhen, and of course Shanghai. Each city has a completely different atmosphere and gives a unique perspective on modern China.

For cultural and historical experiences, Nanjing, Xian and Beijing are must-visits, offering important historical sites and a deeper understanding of China’s past and present.

Other fascinating destinations include Harbin, especially during winter when it hosts the world-famous Harbin International Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival, featuring enormous illuminated ice sculptures and castles. Sanya and Yunnan are also very popular during the winter months, especially for those who prefer warmer weather and want to escape the cold.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be curious, ask questions, invite them to stuff with your (exchange) friends

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Hard to say, because the real answer is everything: the people, the food, the nature, the culture, etc.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be open-minded. Do not go on exchange if you are not willing to challenge your own perspective and embrace something different from what you are used to. China can feel very different from Denmark in many ways, and the experience becomes much more rewarding if you approach it with curiosity rather than comparison.
2. Talk to the locals. Chinese students and local people are incredibly kind, genuine, and helpful if you make the effort to start a conversation. Even with language barriers, people are often very welcoming, and some of my best experiences came from connecting with local students rather than only staying within the international student circle.
3. Travel as much as possible within China. China is incredibly underrated and has everything—modern megacities, rich history, breathtaking nature, mountains, beaches, and unique regional cultures. Exploring the country gave me a much deeper understanding of both Chinese society and daily life, and it became one of the most valuable parts of my exchange experience.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Refer to some of my earlier answers

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The friendships I made and the stronger sense of connection I developed with China were some of the most valuable outcomes of my exchange. Living there allowed me to gain a much deeper and more nuanced understanding of a country that is often heavily scrutinized and simplified in Western media. Experiencing daily life firsthand gave me perspectives that could never have been gained through news articles or academic reading alone, and it helped me appreciate the complexity of Chinese society, culture, and people far beyond common stereotypes.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: One of the biggest challenges I faced was the language barrier when I became sick and needed to go to the hospital. Communicating medical concerns in a foreign language was stressful, especially in an unfamiliar healthcare system. Fortunately, I had Mandarin-speaking friends who came with me and helped translate, which made the situation much easier and far less overwhelming.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
